descs.t: A federal judge in Alaska has dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit over the state's Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan appears on the ballot beside Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. We walk through what the suit asked for, why it was thrown out, and what happens next.

Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the DOJ's Decoy Dan lawsuit in Alaska, and the department says it is appealing. President Trump says Chuck Schumer and Marc Elias should be held responsible for the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot, while one poll shows Peltola and Sullivan tied at 50 percent. We look at how a duplicate name could matter under ranked choice.

Two men named Dan Sullivan are on Alaska's Senate ballot, a court just tossed the DOJ's attempt to step in, and Trump calls it election fraud at the highest level. With the race tied in one poll, every confused ballot could count. We break down the fight, the appeal, and whether voters can trust the result.

intro.plain: A federal judge in Alaska has thrown out the Justice Department's lawsuit over the Senate race, where a second Dan Sullivan is on the ballot next to the real Senator Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola. The DOJ says it will appeal. So what was the suit about, and does it change anything before the vote? Chat, have you ever seen two candidates with the same name on one ballot?

descs.t: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on the eve of Tuesday's vote. Reports say her chief of staff and other staff resigned, and former Congressman Hansen Clarke has also backed Rogers. We walk through what happened and where the race stands.

Haley Stevens' endorsement of Mike Rogers has split Michigan Democrats ahead of Tuesday's Senate vote. Her chief of staff and others resigned, Bernie Sanders and Gavin Newsom rallied behind Abdul El-Sayed, and his campaign says it raised $1.2 million in four hours. We look at who gains and who loses.

A Democratic congresswoman has crossed the aisle in Michigan's Senate race, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed. Her own party turned on her, Trump said he would love to have her, and another Michigan Democrat followed her lead. We break down why she did it and what it means for Tuesday.

intro.plain: Big news out of Michigan on the eve of the vote. Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers. Reports say her chief of staff and others resigned over it, and former Congressman Hansen Clarke has backed Rogers too. So tell me in the chat: does a crossover endorsement this late actually move votes?

A Tucker Carlson post claiming Trump could be days from a nuclear strike on Iran spread to tens of millions, and critics from Laura Loomer to Hans Mahncke call it a hoax timed for the midterms. Several outlets report Trump clashing with Netanyahu over a renewed attack on the Islamic Republic. We look at who is saying what and why it matters now.

descs.t: Texas early voting closed with 7,705,786 votes, about 74.1% of projected final turnout, ahead of Tuesday's Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. Recent polls range from Paxton ahead by 0.6 to Talarico ahead by 4. We go through the numbers and what they can and cannot tell us.

With 7.7 million early votes in, Texas heads into Tuesday with a Senate race the polls cannot agree on: Trafalgar has Ken Paxton up 0.6, YouGov has James Talarico up 4. The governor's race between Greg Abbott and Gina Hinojosa also looks close in some polls. We look at where Texas really stands.

Texas turned out in near presidential numbers before Election Day, and Ken Paxton's Senate race against James Talarico is within a point in one final poll. Democrats talk about flipping the state, Republicans say Latino men are sticking with Trump. We break down the early vote and what it means for Tuesday.

descs.t: Ukraine's General Staff says Russian forces used the humanitarian ceasefire in occupied Oleshky to rotate troops and replenish ammunition, and Sky News drone footage appears to show heavy equipment moving in during the pause. The mission evacuated nearly 800 people. We go through what the footage shows and what happened when the truce ended.

A humanitarian pause in occupied Oleshky got nearly 800 civilians out, but Ukraine's General Staff says Russia used the same window to reinforce, and Sky News footage appears to back that up. Reports say Kherson was struck again soon after the truce ended. We look at why Ukrainian soldiers warned this would happen and what it means for any future deal.

Ukraine agreed to a pause so civilians could escape Oleshky. According to Ukraine's General Staff and Sky News drone footage, Russian forces used it to bring in armor, troops and ammunition, and Kherson came under fire again right after. We break down the evidence and what it says about trusting Putin's word on any ceasefire.

descs.t: The Trump administration has filed an emergency appeal asking the Supreme Court to stop California from counting about 20,000 mail ballots that federal officials flagged as likely cast by noncitizens. Reuters, NPR, CNN and others are reporting the case. We walk through what was filed and what the court is being asked to do.

The Justice Department has taken its fight with California over roughly 20,000 mail ballots to the Supreme Court, saying the state refused to work with the federal government on noncitizen voting. California's ballots now wait on the court. We look at both sides of the case and what happens next.

Who gets to vote in an American election is now in front of the Supreme Court. The Trump administration wants about 20,000 California mail ballots set aside, saying federal checks flagged them as likely from noncitizens. We break down the claim, the state's refusal and what is at stake for every lawful vote.

intro.plain: Breaking legal fight right before Election Day. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting about 20,000 mail ballots that federal officials flagged as likely from noncitizens. The Justice Department says California refused to cooperate. So, chat: should those ballots be counted while the case is decided?
